name: Savannah Ghosts
description: A self-guided evening walk through the documented history and ghost legends of Savannah's Historic District.

stops.name: Forsyth Park Fountain

viewpoint.description: Public sidewalk on East Gaston Street along the southern edge of Forsyth Park, beside the fountain.

stops.narration: You are standing on the public sidewalk on East Gaston Street along the southern edge of Forsyth Park, looking toward the white cast-iron fountain that has watched over the park since 1858. The fountain was gifted to the city by the city council and funded by a local merchant, and it became the beating heart of Savannah's public life. In the nineteenth century the park was the terminus of a long promenade that stretched from the river to the cemetery, and families came here to walk, hear bands play, and children chase pigeons around the fountain. The park's live oaks predate the park itself, and their moss has been the backdrop for everything from wartime nurses to peacocks, which once roamed free. The history here is documented and the stories around it are legend, told by families who kept passing down what they saw on summer evenings. No haunting is claimed as fact; the fountain simply kept doing its work while the city around it changed. Look closely at how the fountain is oriented toward the park rather than the street, and you will understand how much this green space meant to the people who built it and the people who still gather beneath the oaks.

funFacts.text: The Forsyth Park fountain dates to 1858 and was funded by the city council.
Live oak trees in the park predate the park itself and are over two hundred years old.

quizzes.question: In what year was the Forsyth Park fountain installed?
quizzes.explanation: The cast-iron fountain was installed in 1858 and has been the park's centerpiece since.

stops.lookFor: Watch how the fountain faces the park, not the street, and where the moss-draped oaks gather.
stops.discuss: What does a shared public space owe its regulars who never knew it would outlive them?
stops.challenge: Find one live oak older than the park itself.

extraStory.text: The fountain arrived in 1858, paid for by the city council and given to the people. Before the park became a formal square, Savannah's promenade ran from the river to the squares and the fountain was its terminus. The live oaks around it were already ancient when the park was laid out. Wartime nurses walked the paths, band concerts filled the air, and children fed pigeons at the fountain's edge. The documented history is calm and lovely; the legends are what locals added afterwards, and both belong in a walk like this. A careful walker can feel the century and a half of afternoon strolls that have passed this exact spot, and can read the park as a civic room that has never stopped being used.

stops.name: Confederate Monument in Forsyth Park

viewpoint.description: Public sidewalk on East Gaston Street at the edge of Forsyth Park, beside the monument's base.

stops.narration: You are standing on the public sidewalk on East Gaston Street, looking at the Confederate monument standing in the heart of Forsyth Park. The monument has been part of the landscape since the 1870s, and it has been a quiet site of civic memory for more than a century. The walk you are on is not about the monument's bronze; it is about the people who passed this corner with it in view. After the Civil War, Savannah's families had to reckon with what the war meant for the living as much as for the dead, and this square was where that reckoning happened in open air. The documented record is clear about dates and facts; the stories told here are about memory, not verified sightings. Keep your visit respectful, and treat every plaque as history and every whisper as a story. Savannah's public memory has always been layered, and the plaza around the monument is one place where the layers sit side by side in plain view.

funFacts.text: The Confederate monument in Forsyth Park was erected in the 1870s.

quizzes.question: The Forsyth Park fountain was installed in what year?
quizzes.explanation: The cast-iron fountain was installed in 1858.

stops.lookFor: Notice how the monument and the fountain face the same open green.
stops.discuss: How should a public monument hold grief without turning it into spectacle?
stops.challenge: Name one kind of documented history you saw in the park today.

extraStory.text: The park and its monuments were dedicated in the nineteenth century, and the fountain arrived in 1858. The square became the social heart of Savannah, where families strolled, bands played, and children ran. What the monuments mean now is a story told by each generation, not a fact frozen in bronze. The walk continues toward the squares of the Historic District. A reader who watches the park at dusk will see people pausing at the monument and at the fountain with the same ease, and the history here stays with them whether or not any ghost is real.

stops.name: Monterey Square

viewpoint.description: Public sidewalk on the north side of Monterey Square, the second square of the Historic District.

stops.narration: You are standing on the public sidewalk on the north side of Monterey Square, the second of Savannah's original squares. The square was laid out in the original 1733 planning of James Oglethorpe's city and named for the Scottish financier and merchant John Monro, though Savannah records show the name was later changed to honor the ship's captain who brought it to the colony. The square is bordered by residential and civic buildings, and it holds the Mercer-Williams House on its eastern edge, where local legend says the spirits of Civil War-era residents still walk. The walk you are leading is a story about a place and its people, and the documented history of the square is well recorded; the haunting stories told from this corner belong to folklore and to memory. Keep them labeled as stories, and keep your footing on the public sidewalk. The square is one of the prettiest public rooms in Savannah, and it is easy to see why people have told stories about it for generations.

funFacts.text: Monterey Square was laid out in Savannah's original 1733 planning by James Oglethorpe.

quizzes.question: Who laid out Savannah's original 1733 street plan?
quizzes.explanation: James Oglethorpe, the founder of Georgia, laid out the original plan in 1733.

stops.lookFor: Look for the square's park benches and the wrought-iron fencing that marks the edge.
stops.discuss: How do squares work as civic rooms in Savannah?
stops.challenge: Count how many of the square's sides are houses versus parkland.

extraStory.text: Savannah's original plan placed squares at the heart of the city, and Monterey Square is one of the original squares. The names of the squares and the houses around them carry stories that families have retold for generations. The Mercer-Williams House is one such story, tied to documented events and to local legend. Both can be true at once, and a walk that keeps legend clearly labeled is a walk that respects the history. The square is a place where the past is not behind a museum door but sitting in plain air among the oaks and the iron fence, and that is exactly what makes Savannah's squares so memorable to every visitor who pauses here.

stops.name: Colonial Park Cemetery

viewpoint.description: Public sidewalk on Oglethorpe Avenue facing the cemetery wall, outside the gate.

stops.narration: You are standing on the public sidewalk on Oglethorpe Avenue, looking at the whitewashed wall of Colonial Park Cemetery across the street. The cemetery has served Savannah since the 1750s and holds graves of many of the city's earliest colonists, including records of the dead from the wars and epidemics of the eighteenth century. The documented history is well supported by the cemetery's records, and the legends that surround it, about restless spirits and unexplained visits, are stories told by the living. The cemetery is a working burial ground and a public park, and the walker stands on the public sidewalk while reading what the cemetery keeps. Treat the rest as folklore, labeled and clear. The wall you see is a record of a city that buried its people close to the center of daily life, and the graves inside belong to the families who built the squares and houses we have been walking past all evening.

funFacts.text: Colonial Park Cemetery has served Savannah since the 1750s.
The cemetery holds graves of Savannah's earliest colonists.

quizzes.question: In what decade did Colonial Park Cemetery begin serving Savannah?
quizzes.explanation: The cemetery opened in the 1750s, long before Savannah grew into the city it is today.

stops.lookFor: Look at the cemetery wall from the public sidewalk, and notice the gate is closed.
stops.discuss: How should a walking tour handle a place where grief is still active?
stops.challenge: Spot the section of the wall you think holds the oldest documented graves.

extraStory.text: The cemetery began in the eighteenth century and remains a working burial ground. Families still come here, and the documented history of its graves is real. The ghost stories that visitors and locals tell about the cemetery are a separate layer, a folklore of place rather than a record of fact. A careful walk names both layers clearly, and this one does. The walker stands at the gate and reads the wall, and the story is about the people who were buried here before the city grew large and crowded around them. The respect a tour owes this place is to keep the facts and the legends in their own lanes, and this stop tries to do exactly that.

stops.name: Sorrel-Weed House

viewpoint.description: Public sidewalk on Abercorn Street in front of the Sorrel-Weed House, across the street from the iron gate.

stops.narration: You are standing on the public sidewalk on Abercorn Street, across from the iron gate of the Sorrel-Weed House. The house was built in the 1850s and later served as the home of the artist and writer Cornelia Sorrel Weems, whose family gave the house its name. The documented history is rich and real, including the family's letters and the house's place in the city's art life. The legends attached to Savannah homes often come from the city's habit of layering one story over another, and the whispers about this house are part of that tradition rather than a verified haunting. The walker should keep the house on the far side of the public street, and the story in view from the sidewalk. The iron gate is closed, and the house is private property, so the walker's place is here on the public sidewalk where the story can be told without trespass or trouble. Savannah has always loved a house with a story, and this one has more than its share, each story adding a little color to the next.

funFacts.text: The Sorrel-Weed House was built in the 1850s.

quizzes.question: The Sorrel-Weed House was built in what decade?
quizzes.explanation: The house dates to the 1850s and was later home to Cornelia Sorrel Weems.

stops.lookFor: Look at the iron gate and the windows from the public sidewalk.
stops.discuss: How do documented family lives become local legends?
stops.challenge: Find the house's name on the gate and read the date.

extraStory.text: The house took its name from the family that lived there across generations, and its rooms have held letters, art, and the ordinary furniture of a long life. The stories people tell about the house after dark are local legends, part of Savannah's folklore rather than its records. The walk keeps them in that lane. The walker stands across the street and reads the iron gate, and the history of the family who lived here is real, documented in letters and records. The whispers that follow the house around town are a separate thing, a folklore that Savannah enjoys and retells. This stop is about holding both at once, and keeping the legend clearly labeled so nobody mistakes a good story for a fact.

stops.name: Andrew Low House

viewpoint.description: Public sidewalk on Abercorn Street in front of the Andrew Low House, across the street from the iron gate.

stops.narration: You are standing on the public sidewalk on Abercorn Street, across from the iron gate of the Andrew Low House. The house was built in the 1850s and was home to Andrew Low, a cotton merchant and philanthropist whose family were among Savannah's most prominent families. The documented history of the house, including its letters and its place in the city's mercantile life, is real and well sourced. The legends that grew around Savannah's great houses are stories told by visitors and by the families who stayed, and they are folklore, not evidence. The walker stands on the public sidewalk, and the house stands across it, and the story moves between them. The Andrew Low House is a place of real letters and real business, and the tour honors the family who lived there while keeping the ghostly whispers at a polite distance. The sidewalk is the walker's place, and the house is private, so the walker stays put and lets the story do the visiting.

funFacts.text: The Andrew Low House was built in the 1850s and was home to Andrew Low.

quizzes.question: The Andrew Low House was built in what decade?

stops.lookFor: Look at the double piazza that runs across the front of the house.
stops.discuss: How does a city's real history feed its legends?
stops.challenge: Notice the iron gate and the piazza behind it.

extraStory.text: The Low House was a real home for a real family, and its letters are preserved. The ghosts that people speak of are the stories they carry from the city, and they are stories about the place as much as about the people. The walk keeps the two separate, which is the whole point of this tour. The walker stands across the street from a house that is private property, and the piazza and gate belong to the family who lives here now. What the walker takes away is the story of the family who built it and the folklore the city added around them. Both are welcome here, as long as the walker stays on the public sidewalk and keeps the legend where it belongs.

stops.name: Davenport House

viewpoint.description: Public sidewalk on East State Street in front of the Davenport House, across from the iron gate.

stops.narration: You are standing on the public sidewalk on East State Street, across from the iron gate of the Davenport House. The house dates to the 1820s and was home to Dorothy and William Davenport, who were early collectors of what would become the city's folklore. The documented history of the house is real, and the legends attached to Savannah's historic homes are real in their telling, even when they are not in their fact. The walk here is a reminder that a tour can hold both: the letters and records that support a story, and the story itself. Keep the walker on the public sidewalk, and keep the legend where it belongs. The Davenport House is one of the earliest and most carefully documented houses in the Historic District, and it was the family who lived here that helped turn Savannah's everyday life into the stories the city tells about itself today.

funFacts.text: The Davenport House dates to the 1820s.

quizzes.question: The Davenport House dates to what decade?

stops.lookFor: Look at the garden and the iron gate from the public sidewalk.
stops.discuss: Why do so many tours start with a house full of stories?
stops.challenge: Look for the house's name on the iron gate.

extraStory.text: The house was home to the Davenports, who collected and told stories about Savannah, and the city has never stopped telling them. The documented record of the house exists; the legends around it are the city's conversation with its own past. Both are welcome here, as long as the walk keeps them in their proper places. The walker stands on the public sidewalk while the house sits behind its iron gate, and the story is about the family who lived here and the city that grew up around them. The Davenports were collectors of the city's stories, and this tour is a small way of continuing that work, keeping the facts and the folklore side by side without letting one stand in for the other.

stops.name: The Pirates' House

viewpoint.description: Public sidewalk on East Broad Street in front of the Pirates' House, beside the restaurant's sidewalk entrance.

stops.narration: You are standing on the public sidewalk on East Broad Street, in front of the Pirates' House. The building dates to the early nineteenth century and was long known as a tavern and boarding house where sailors and pirates were said to have met. The documented history of the building's use is real, and the pirate stories are legend, told by tavern keepers and by visitors who came for a good story. The walk keeps the two apart: what the building was, and what people said it was. The walker stands on the public sidewalk, and the story stands on the far side of the door. The Pirates' House is one of Savannah's oldest buildings and one of its most storied, and the tour is careful to say what the building really was while letting the pirate legends remain legends. The walker is on the sidewalk, the tavern is private, and the story is told from where the walker stands.

funFacts.text: The Pirates' House building dates to the early nineteenth century.

quizzes.question: The Pirates' House dates to what century?
quizzes.explanation: The building dates to the early 1800s.

stops.lookFor: Look at the two-story porch and the sidewalk that runs beside it.
stops.discuss: How does a city keep its real past from being swallowed by its stories?
stops.challenge: Spot the building number on the facade.

extraStory.text: The tavern at the corner is a real building with a real history, and the pirate tales that cling to it are a legend of the river trade. The walk has come to the end of its loop, and the story it tells is about how a place keeps both its facts and its fables in view. The walker stands on the public sidewalk, and the building behind its doors is private, so the story is told from where the walker stands without crossing the line. Savannah has always loved a building with a story, and this one has a story that visitors have told for generations. This tour keeps the two apart, letting the documented history stand while the legend stays a legend, and the walker can leave here knowing the difference.

stops.name: Wright Square

viewpoint.description: Public sidewalk on the edge of Wright Square, looking across the open park.

stops.narration: You are standing on the public sidewalk on the edge of Wright Square, the largest of Savannah's original squares, laid out in 1801. The square was named for Martha Wright, who donated the land for the city's first orphanage. The documented history of the square and its uses is clear, and the legends attached to Savannah's squares are part of the city's storytelling tradition. This is the last stop of the walk, and the walker has come full circle through the Historic District. The documented history is the spine; the legends are the color. Both are welcome on a walk that keeps the walker on public sidewalks and the stories honest. The square is a place where Savannah's civic life has played out for two centuries, and the walker who stands here can see the whole district in a new light, knowing how much history and how much storytelling share the same public ground.

funFacts.text: Wright Square was laid out in 1801 and named for Martha Wright.

quizzes.question: Wright Square was laid out in what year?
quizzes.explanation: The square was laid out in 1801.

stops.lookFor: Look across the square at the monuments and the trees.
stops.discuss: What makes a place worth telling a ghost story about?

extraStory.text: The square began as a gift of land for an orphanage, and over the years it became a public park. The documented history of the square is quiet and civic. The legends that surround Savannah's squares are local lore, and the walk closes by naming both without letting either become the other. The walker has come full circle, and the story it tells is about how a city keeps its facts and its fables side by side. The square is the last stop of the evening, and the walker who stands here can look back across the district and see how much of Savannah's charm is built from real history and real storytelling, each one welcome in its own lane. This tour has tried to keep them apart all evening, and it ends where it began, on a public sidewalk with the stories in view.
